title: Sumerian flood story as the source of Noah

tellings.quote: if you read the Epic of Gilgamesh the atrasis and then you compare the flood story it's like literally almost identical to Genesis
Throw down the house, build a ship,
Carry grain of every kind into the ship.
The cattle of the field, the beasts of the field, all handicraftsmen I made them go up into it.
The storm raged, and the cyclone overwhelmed the land.
The mountain of Nisir held the ship, it let it not move.
I brought out a dove and let her go free.
I brought out a swallow and let her go free.
I brought out a raven and let her go free.
She ate, she pecked in the ground, she croaked, she came not back.

plain: Noah's flood in Genesis has a close older relative in the flood tale of ancient Mesopotamia, says the researcher Matt LaCroix. He tells Michels that if you read the Epic of Gilgamesh and the Atrahasis, another Mesopotamian flood poem, and compare them with Genesis, "it's like literally almost identical". If he is right, the Bible's story came from an older one, and perhaps from a flood that people remembered. The tablet speaks for itself in E. A. Wallis Budge's translation, published by the British Museum in 1920. There, the god Ea warns one man: "Throw down the house, build a ship", and "Carry grain of every kind into the ship." The survivor, Uta-Napishtim, says: "The cattle of the field, the beasts of the field... I made them go up into it." Then "The storm raged", and "The mountain of Nisir held the ship." He sends out a dove, then a swallow, then a raven, which "came not back", and afterwards he offers a sacrifice. That order of events, a warning, a boat, animals, a storm, a mountain and the birds, is what LaCroix sets beside Noah, and the different names neither help nor hurt the comparison. What the tablet alone cannot settle is which way the story travelled, whether both versions come from an older shared one, and whether a real flood lies behind it.

discussion.by: The Epic of Gilgamish, Tablet XI (translated by E. A. Wallis Budge in The Babylonian Story of the Deluge)
discussion.text: In Budge's translation of the Eleventh Tablet, the god Ea warns one man, the "man of Shurippak": "Throw down the house, build a ship", and "The dimensions thereof shall be measured"; he takes "all my family and kinsfolk" aboard with the beasts of the field, the ship comes to rest on a mountain, he sends out a dove, a swallow and a raven in turn, and after landing he offers a sacrifice and "The gods smelt the sweet savour." These are the elements the tellers set beside Noah's story, and the tablet's own names (Uta-Napishtim, the mountain of Nisir) count neither for nor against a borrowing. What the tablet alone cannot settle is which way the story travelled, whether both tellings come from an older common one, and whether a real flood is remembered in it; the comparison with Genesis is the tellers'.
